terms.definition: The tightening and flattening of the dome-shaped diaphragm muscle that kicks off one breathing cycle.
terms.function: Enlarges the chest cavity by pulling the diaphragm's dome downward, dropping the pressure inside the lungs so the cycle can begin.
terms.whereItIs: At the base of the thoracic cavity, on the diaphragm dome beneath the lungs.
terms.whyItMatters: It's the trigger for every breath — without the diaphragm contracting first, the lungs have no reason to expand.

terms.definition: The outward and downward stretch of the elastic lungs as they fill the extra space made by the diaphragm.
terms.function: Lets the lungs' internal volume grow to match the enlarged chest cavity, which is what actually drops the air pressure inside the airway.
terms.whereItIs: The mid-outer surface of the lungs, most visible at the widest point of the larger, three-lobe right lung.
terms.whyItMatters: Lung expansion is a passive response, not an active pull — it's the direct link between the diaphragm's motion and air actually moving.

terms.definition: Drawing air into the lungs through the nose or mouth, down the trachea, and into the bronchi.
terms.function: Moves fresh, oxygen-rich air from outside the body down into the airway and toward the alveoli, driven by the pressure drop from lung expansion.
terms.whereItIs: The top of the trachea, just below where it meets the throat.
terms.whyItMatters: Inhaling is the delivery step — it's how oxygen physically gets from the outside world to where gas exchange can happen.

terms.definition: The swap of oxygen and carbon dioxide across the thin walls of the alveoli, between the air and the blood.
terms.function: Lets oxygen diffuse from the air into the bloodstream and carbon dioxide diffuse from the blood into the air, using no pump — just diffusion.
terms.whereItIs: At the tips of the smallest airways, on the zoomed alveoli-cluster inset near the lower-outer edge of the right lung.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the actual point of breathing — every other stage exists to get air to this exchange surface and take the swapped gases away again.

terms.definition: Pushing carbon-dioxide-rich air back out of the lungs as the diaphragm relaxes and the chest cavity shrinks.
terms.function: Clears out carbon dioxide-rich air so the next inhale can bring in a fresh supply of oxygen.
terms.whereItIs: The lower trachea / upper bronchi junction, just above where the airway splits into the two lungs.
terms.whyItMatters: Exhaling is mostly passive elastic recoil, not a separate active push — understanding that helps explain why breathing normally feels effortless at rest.

terms.definition: A dome-shaped sheet of muscle below the lungs; it contracts and flattens downward to power inhaling and relaxes upward to help push air out.
terms.function: Acts as the primary engine of breathing by changing the volume of the chest cavity with every contraction and relaxation.
terms.whereItIs: Anchored to the lower ribs, forming the floor of the chest cavity beneath the lungs.
terms.whyItMatters: It's why singers, swimmers, and athletes train 'diaphragm control' — a stronger, more controlled diaphragm means more efficient breathing.

terms.definition: The windpipe — the main tube that carries air from your throat down toward the lungs.
terms.function: Provides a single, rigid, ring-reinforced passage for air to travel from the throat down to where it splits into the bronchi.
terms.whereItIs: Running down the front of the neck and upper chest, splitting into the left and right bronchi partway down.
terms.whyItMatters: Its cartilage rings keep it from collapsing with every breath, so air can always get through.

terms.definition: The two large branches where the trachea splits, one leading into each lung, before dividing further into smaller airways.
terms.function: Route incoming air from the single trachea into each lung, then keep branching into progressively smaller tubes toward the alveoli.
terms.whereItIs: Just below the middle of the chest, where the trachea forks into a left and right branch.
terms.whyItMatters: This branching is why one windpipe can serve two lungs, and it's a common site for airway narrowing in conditions like asthma.

terms.definition: Tiny balloon-like air sacs at the very end of the airway branches, wrapped in thin blood vessels, where oxygen and carbon dioxide are swapped.
terms.function: Provide the enormous, thin-walled surface area needed for oxygen and carbon dioxide to diffuse between air and blood.
terms.whereItIs: Clustered like grapes at the terminal tips of the smallest bronchioles, deep inside the lungs.
terms.whyItMatters: Each pair of lungs has a few hundred million alveoli — that huge surface area is what makes gas exchange fast enough to keep up with the body's needs.

terms.definition: The pair of elastic, sponge-like organs that expand and recoil with every breath, housing the airway branches and alveoli.
terms.function: Provide the housing and elastic recoil for the entire breathing cycle — expanding to draw air in and springing back to help push it out.
terms.whereItIs: Filling most of the chest cavity, protected by the ribcage, with the right lung (3 lobes) larger than the left (2 lobes, to make room for the heart).
terms.whyItMatters: Because lungs are passive elastic tissue rather than active muscle, understanding them explains why the diaphragm — not the lungs themselves — is what actually drives breathing.
